reading.title: Describing a storage room
reading.text: The learner studies an empty storage-room plan. A wine rack supports bottles. Temperature control and humidity control regulate different environmental conditions. A stone wall is part of the room; the cellar door provides access. A tasting table serves organized comparison, while dim lighting describes low illumination without guaranteeing safe movement. Ventilation exchanges air, and insulation limits heat transfer. A wine fridge provides controlled bottle storage. Horizontal storage means keeping bottles on their sides where suitable for the closure and product. Bottle names the container; cork names a closure, capsule a neck covering, and label printed identification information. The learner asks what the actual storage records require. The lesson provides words for describing the room rather than a universal temperature, humidity or storage prescription.

reading.title: Reading inventory and equipment records
reading.text: The cellar worksheet separates records from serving equipment. Vintage usually identifies the grape-harvest year in this context. A bin number identifies a storage location, while the cellar book records items and their locations. Inventory names the stock or its record; collection refers to a grouped set of bottles. A decanter is a serving vessel, and a wine glass is a drinking glass. A corkscrew removes corks; wine opener is the broader tool label. An aerator exposes liquid to air, a wine stopper closes an opened bottle, and a wine pourer controls flow. A Champagne flute is a slender tall-bowled glass. An ice bucket holds ice or cools a bottle, and a wine thermometer measures temperature. The learner interprets the list without assuming that equipment guarantees preservation or product quality.

reading.title: Interpreting regional names
reading.text: The geography worksheet treats names as regions rather than bottle-color clues. Bordeaux, Burgundy and Champagne are French regions associated with wine production. Champagne also has a protected product designation; not every sparkling wine is Champagne. Tuscany is in Italy. Napa Valley is in California, while Rioja is in Spain. Barossa Valley is in South Australia, and Mendoza is in Argentina. The Douro Valley in Portugal is associated with Port and other wines. Mosel names a major German wine-growing region along the Moselle River. A regional name can have several related uses, so the learner reads the context. A generic vineyard photograph cannot establish origin or protected status. Maps and verified records support geographical claims without requiring a product purchase or consumption.
